The chessboard has $40 \times 60 = 2400$ squares. A knight's graph is bipartite, meaning it can be colored such that knights only move between colors. On a $40 \times 60$ board, there are $2400 / 2 = 1200$ white squares and 1200 black squares. Horst's knights must form an independent set in the knight's graph. By only placing knights on white squares, Horst ensures that no two knights attack each other, as knights only attack squares of the opposite color.

In each turn, Horst places a knight and then Queenie places a queen. The game ends when someone cannot move. To minimize the number of knights Horst places, Queenie should aim to occupy squares that Horst wants to use. If Horst only uses white squares, Queenie should occupy as many white squares as possible. 

In each turn, Horst takes one white square, and Queenie takes one square of her choice. If Queenie has no restrictions on her queen's placement (except for occupying an empty square), she can always take a white square as long as one is available. Since there are 1200 white squares and Horst takes one per turn, the game will end after at most $1200 / 2 = 600$ turns if Queenie always takes a white square. In this case, Horst would have placed 600 knights.

If Queenie *is* restricted (i.e., she cannot place a queen on a square attacked by another queen), the number of queens she can place is limited (at most $\min(40, 60) = 40$). If the game ends because she is blocked, Horst would have placed only 40 knights. Since 600 is a candidate answer and 40 is not, the "no restrictions" interpretation is the most likely, leading to $K = 600$. Even if she *is* restricted, Horst could still ensure at least 600 knights if the game only ended when he couldn't move, but since the game ends when "somebody" cannot move, the "no restrictions" interpretation is the only one that makes 600 the correct answer.

Thus, the maximal $K$ is 600.
